1-1.text: Part one. Charges in atoms. ... Everything is made of tiny atoms. Inside each atom are even tinier particles.

1-2.text: Protons have a positive charge. Electrons have a negative charge. Neutrons have no charge at all.

1-3.text: Protons and neutrons are held tightly in the centre of the atom, the nucleus. Electrons are on the outside, and some can be rubbed off.

1-4.text: Most things have the same number of positive and negative charges. They cancel out, so the object is neutral: it has no overall charge.

2-1.text: Part two. Charging by rubbing. ... Rub a balloon on your hair. The rubbing moves some electrons from your hair onto the balloon.

2-2.text: The balloon has gained electrons, so it has more negative charges than positive ones. It is now negatively charged.

2-3.text: Your hair has lost electrons, so it has more positive charges than negative ones. It is now positively charged.

2-4.text: Only electrons move. Protons are stuck in the nucleus. So an object becomes positive by losing electrons, never by gaining protons.

3-1.text: Part three. Attract and repel. ... Charged objects push or pull on each other without touching. This is a non-contact force.

3-2.text: Like charges repel. Two negative balloons push each other apart. Two positive charges repel too.

3-3.text: Opposite charges attract. A negative balloon and a positive balloon pull towards each other.

3-4.text: The space around a charged object where it pushes or pulls other charges is its electric field. The force is stronger close to the object and weaker further away.

4-1.text: Part four. Sticky balloons. ... A charged balloon can stick to a wall, even though the wall is not charged. How?

4-2.text: The negative balloon pushes electrons in the wall's surface a little way back. That leaves the surface slightly positive, and opposite charges attract.

4-3.text: The same thing happens when a charged rod picks up tiny bits of paper. The bits are so light that the pull lifts them up.

5-1.text: Part five. Sparks and lightning. ... Shuffle across a carpet and charge can build up on you.

5-2.text: Touch a metal door handle and the charge suddenly flows away through the metal, which is a conductor. You feel a tiny shock and may even see a spark.

5-3.text: Lightning is a giant spark. Charge builds up in storm clouds until it jumps to the ground or to another cloud.

5-4.text: Tall buildings have a lightning conductor: a thick metal strip that gives the charge a safe path down to the ground.
